items.title: Why Burger King Has A Completely Different Name In Australia
items.description:
Burger King has thousands of restaurants serving the iconic Whopper in countries all over the world. But in Australia, as they often are, things are a bit different and Burger King isn’t called Burger King... it's called Hungry Jack's. So what happened? 

On this episode of Weird History Food, we take a look at the fast food business in the land down under to explain why Burger King doesn't use its more famous name in Australia and how the Whopper survived under a brand name designed for a panca
items.why_watch: The short answer is a local franchise already held the 'Burger King' trademark when the chain arrived in Australia — but the full story involves legal battles, a scrappy independent operator, and a corporate compromise that's held for decades. It's a clean case study in how brand identity can be hijacked by timing and trademark law.

items.title: Life Below 4,000 Meters: What NOAA Found Under Alaska
items.description:
More than 4,000 meters beneath the surface, NOAA researchers explored the Kodiak Seep in the Gulf of Alaska, encountering strange deep-sea life including fish, sea pens, corals, anemones, sea cucumbers, and a collected sea urchin.

Footage: NOAA Ocean Exploration. Independently edited and produced

#deepsea  #deepoceanlife  #oceanexploration  #deepseacreature  #marinelife  #noaa  #alaska  #deepseaexploration  #deepsealife
items.why_watch: NOAA's footage from the Kodiak Seep is the real draw here — methane-fed coral gardens and ghostly sea cucumbers at 4,000 meters are the kind of thing that makes Earth feel genuinely alien. The editing keeps the pacing tight, letting the imagery do the work without overselling it.

discovery_articles.title: Palm Temple in Bristol, England
discovery_articles.snippet: Bristol has no shortage of churches, but one of its strangest temples is devoted to nature. Outside the University of Bristol’s School of Chemistry, artist Luke Jerram’s Palm Temple resembles a futuristic chapel made of wood and stained glass. Created in 2020 to celebrate the 600th anniversary of Brunelleschi’s famous dome in Florence, it eventually found a permanent home in Jerram’s native Bristol, where he donated it to the university.

discovery_articles.title: The Prince of the Lilies Fresco in Heraklion, Greece
discovery_articles.snippet: The Prince of the Lilies is one of the signature images of Minoan Crete, reproduced on postcards, book covers, and museum posters worldwide: a slender, muscular figure wearing a crown of lilies and peacock feathers, striding forward through a garden, one hand on his chest. It's usually presented as a king, sometimes a priest-king, ruling from Knossos around 1500 BCE. The problem is that almost none of that figure actually survived.

discovery_articles.title: The Fire Captain's Stone in Helsinki, Finland
discovery_articles.snippet: In the courtyard of central Helsinki's oldest surviving wooden house, a rough-hewn cube of reddish granite sits low in the gravel, flat-topped enough to double as a seat. For decades it was the favorite perch of Alexander Wickholm, the fire captain ( ruiskumestari , literally "hose master"), who liked to smoke his pipe there while keeping an eye on the yard. Wickholm died in 1896.
